chunks.title: POAG: signs & differential
chunks.tldr: Silent until late. Open angle, glaucomatous disc: rim thinning (inferior > superior: ISNT broken), notch, Drance haemorrhage, RNFL defect, C/D asymmetry >0.2, bayoneting, DDLS. Fields: nasal step, arcuate, paracentral — respect the horizontal midline. ~Half have IOP ≤21 at a single check.
points: DDx open angle: OHT, physiological cup (big disc, static), secondary OAG (PXF, pigment, steroid, recession, uveitis, raised EVP), NTG, old static damage.
Optic atrophy: pallor > cupping, poor colour/VA, fields respecting vertical midline → neuro.
Drusen: uncupped, calcified on B-scan/CT, autofluorescent.
Closed angle with PAS → chronic angle closure.
chunks.hook: Glaucoma cups; neuro pales.

cards.q: Disc haemorrhage crossing the margin — name and significance?
cards.a: Drance haemorrhage; marker of active/progressive glaucoma.

cards.q: Field defect respecting the vertical midline suggests?
cards.a: Chiasmal or retrochiasmal lesion, not glaucoma.

chunks.title: POAG: workup & red flags
chunks.tldr: Risks: age, African descent, family history, myopia, diabetes, thin CCT, BP extremes. Baseline: VA, RAPD, IOP (applanation), gonioscopy, dilated disc, disc photos/OCT RNFL + GCL, 24-2 field (10-2 if paracentral/advanced), CCT (avg 535–545 µm; thin under-reads). Investigate further if pallor > cup, field worse than disc, vertical-midline defect, VA/colour loss, unilateral progression with equal IOP.
points: Extra tests: diurnal IOP, B12/folate, ACE, ANA, syphilis, Lyme; ESR/CRP/platelets if GCA possible.
MRI brain/orbits with contrast if neuro suspected.
Medical history guides drops: asthma, COPD, heart block, CHF, renal stones, sulfa allergy.
Ask about past LASIK (thin cornea).
chunks.hook: Thin cornea lies low.

cards.q: Effect of a thin cornea on applanation IOP?
cards.a: Underestimates true IOP (thin CCT is also an independent POAG risk factor).

chunks.title: POAG: treatment & drops
chunks.tldr: Only proven therapy = lower IOP; aim ≥30% below the progression level. Start with one drop in one eye (monocular trial) or SLT (repeatable; great for poor compliance/pigmented TM). Surgery first if advanced + fast progression. Treat without damage if IOP >30 or asymmetry >10.
points: Follow-up: 4–6 weeks after PGA/β-blocker/SLT; any time after 3 days for CAI/α-agonist/miotic.
Stable: IOP/disc 3–6 monthly, fields + OCT 4–12 monthly, gonio yearly.
Progressing? Check compliance first.
Punctal occlusion 10 s or eyes closed 1–2 min cuts systemic absorption.
MIGS for mild–moderate; trab with MMC/5-FU; tube; cyclophotocoagulation.
ALT: 70–80% success, 50% by 2–5 yrs; SLT equivalent but repeatable.

head: Class
Watch out for
rows: Iris darkening (hazel), lashes, periorbitopathy, CME/uveitis; avoid pregnancy
Asthma, COPD, bradycardia, heart block, depression, MG
Renal failure, ↓K⁺, paraesthesia, aplastic anaemia, SJS
Brow ache, RD, myopia, <40 yrs intolerable

chunks.hook: Lower it 30%. One drop, one eye, then compare.

cards.q: Target IOP reduction in POAG?
cards.a: At least 30% below the level at which damage occurred.

cards.q: Brimonidine is contraindicated with which drug class?
cards.a: MAO inhibitors (hypertensive crisis).

chunks.title: Normal-tension glaucoma
chunks.tldr: POAG with IOP always <22. More disc haemorrhages; field defects denser, closer to fixation (dense nasal paracentral). Think vascular: migraine, Raynaud, nocturnal hypotension. Rule out mimics: thin cornea/diurnal spikes, old shock, intermittent angle closure, Posner–Schlossman, old steroid insult, compressive lesion. CNTGS: 30% IOP drop → 5-yr progression 35% → 12%.
points: Workup: colour plates, gonio, diurnal curve, BP incl. 24-h, carotid Doppler, MRI if VA/colour/field atypical.
Brimonidine may beat timolol (LoGTS).
Avoid bedtime antihypertensives — give in the morning.
chunks.hook: Normal pressure, low blood flow — don't drop BP at night.

cards.q: What did the CNTGS show?
cards.a: Lowering IOP ≥30% cut 5-year field progression from 35% to 12%.

chunks.title: Ocular hypertension
chunks.tldr: IOP >21 on ≥2 visits, open normal angle, normal disc/RNFL/field. Treat if >24–30 with risk factors (age, thin CCT, high IOP, disc look, family history). OHTS: 20% IOP drop → conversion 9.5% → 4.4% at 5 years. Repeat abnormal fields (learning effect); OCT may show damage first.
points: Follow like POAG initially; then 6–12 monthly if stable.
Risk calculators help decide treat vs watch.
chunks.hook: OHTS: treatment halves conversion.

cards.q: OHTS 5-year conversion rates treated vs untreated?

chunks.title: Acute angle closure: causes
chunks.tldr: Pain, halos, headache, nausea/vomiting, red eye, fixed mid-dilated pupil, corneal oedema, shallow AC, narrow fellow angle. Primary = pupil block (hyperopes, East Asian, female, older; triggered by dim light, dilation, anticholinergics) or plateau iris. Secondary: PAS, NVG, ICE/PPCD, phacomorphic, microspherophakia, pseudophakic block, topiramate/sulfa (bilateral, myopic shift), choroidal swelling, tumour, suprachoroidal haemorrhage, aqueous misdirection.
points: Acute IOP rise with open angle: uveitic, hyphaema, pigmentary, PXF, lens-related, Posner–Schlossman, retrobulbar haemorrhage, CCF.
Glaukomflecken + iris atrophy = previous attacks.
Clear cornea with glycerin for gonio; gonio both eyes.
Spontaneous arterial pulsations = very urgent.
Angle closure can present with normal IOP after an attack.
chunks.hook: Vomiting + red eye + mid-dilated pupil = gonio now, not a GI consult.

cards.q: Mechanism of topiramate-induced angle closure?
cards.a: Ciliochoroidal effusion rotates the lens–iris diaphragm forward (bilateral, myopic shift) — not pupil block.

cards.q: What are glaukomflecken?
cards.a: Anterior subcapsular lens opacities indicating prior acute angle closure.

chunks.title: Acute angle closure: treatment
chunks.tldr: All topicals (timolol, brimonidine, dorzolamide ± latanoprost ± pilocarpine 1%) up to 3 rounds 15 min apart + acetazolamide 500 mg IV/PO + steroid drop; recheck IOP at 1 h → mannitol 1–2 g/kg IV if needed. Compression gonioscopy may break it; paracentesis drops IOP immediately. Definitive: laser PI once cornea clears (1–5 days) — and the fellow eye (40–80% attack risk in 5–10 yrs).
points: No CAI in sulfa-induced closure or sickle cell; check renal function before CAI/mannitol.
Mannitol: avoid in CHF, renal disease, intracranial bleed.
Pseudophakic/secondary: no pilocarpine; cyclopentolate + phenylephrine.
Topiramate: stop drug, atropine, IV steroids; PI not indicated.
Phacomorphic: remove lens once quiet.
Too hazy for PI → laser the fellow eye first.
PI patent but still closing → plateau iris → iridoplasty; then lens extraction/filter.
Tell relatives: ⅓–½ have occludable angles.
chunks.hook: Drops ×3, Diamox, mannitol — then laser both eyes.

cards.q: Why laser the fellow eye in acute angle closure?
cards.a: 40–80% risk of an attack within 5–10 years.

cards.q: Name two situations where pilocarpine should not be used for angle closure.
cards.a: Pseudophakic/aphakic pupil block and lens-induced/secondary or topiramate closure (can worsen).

chunks.title: Chronic angle closure glaucoma
chunks.tldr: Usually silent. Broad PAS on gonioscopy + glaucomatous disc/field. Causes: creeping appositional closure, repeated subacute attacks, old flat AC. More common in African-descent patients than acute closure. Rx: laser PI (watch IOP spikes), drops, iridoplasty; lens extraction, trab/tube. SLT contraindicated; MIGS usually not possible.
points: Goniosynechiolysis if PAS <6 months old.
chunks.hook: PAS everywhere → no SLT.

cards.q: Why is laser trabeculoplasty contraindicated in CACG?
cards.a: TM isn't accessible and laser can increase angle scarring.

chunks.title: Angle recession glaucoma
chunks.tldr: Years after blunt trauma/hyphaema; unilateral. Gonio: widened ciliary body band, torn iris processes, whiter spur — compare with fellow eye. Rx like POAG but pilocarpine may raise IOP (cuts uveoscleral outflow) and SLT rarely works → often surgery.
points: Watch the other eye — high rate of later OAG.
Recession without glaucoma: yearly checks.
chunks.hook: Old punch, wide band, years later high pressure.

cards.q: Gonioscopic hallmark of angle recession?
cards.a: Abnormally wide ciliary body band (posteriorly displaced iris root).

chunks.title: Inflammatory glaucoma & Posner–Schlossman
chunks.tldr: Inflammatory OAG: lots of cells/flare, trabeculitis → high IOP. Treat inflammation harder (prednisolone q1–6h + cycloplegic) + aqueous suppressants; herpes classically raises IOP. Posner–Schlossman: young–middle age, unilateral recurrent, IOP 40–60 in a white quiet eye, few fine KP, open angle, no synechiae (? CMV). Short steroid course + suppressants; both eyes at risk of chronic OAG.
points: IOP high with active uveitis → more steroid, not less.
High IOP after inflammation settles → think steroid response.
Surgery: tube preferred over trab (trabs fail in uveitis).
Suspect HSV → acyclovir 400 mg 5×/d or valacyclovir 500 mg tds.
PGA/pilocarpine: caution while inflamed.
Fuchs heterochromic: lighter eye, Amsler sign (angle vessels bleed), no PAS.
chunks.hook: Posner–Schlossman: huge pressure, tiny inflammation, white eye.

cards.q: Typical IOP and appearance in glaucomatocyclitic crisis?
cards.a: IOP 40–60 mm Hg with a quiet white eye, few cells, fine KP, open angle.

cards.q: Virus associated with Posner–Schlossman?
cards.a: CMV.

chunks.title: Steroid-response glaucoma
chunks.tldr: IOP rises 2–4 weeks after starting steroid (any route: drops, intravitreal, nasal, inhaled, skin creams). Higher risk: POAG, family history, diabetes, high myopia, African descent, trauma. Dexamethasone/difluprednate worst; FML/loteprednol milder. Rx: stop/taper, weaker steroid, NSAID, IOP drops, SLT, paracentesis, surgery if persists.
points: Always ask about nasal sprays and skin creams.
IOP usually falls after stopping, but can stay high for months.
chunks.hook: Steroids for 2–4 weeks → check the pressure.

cards.q: Onset of steroid IOP response with topical steroids?
cards.a: Typically 2–4 weeks.

chunks.title: Pigment dispersion & pigmentary glaucoma
chunks.tldr: Young myopic men (20–45); concave iris rubs zonules (reverse pupil block). Signs: midperipheral spoke-like TIDs, Krukenberg spindle, homogeneous 360° dense TM pigment, Zentmayer/Scheie line on posterior lens (near pathognomonic), wide angle. IOP spikes/halos after exercise or dilation. Lattice + RD risk.
points: Rx like POAG; pilocarpine reduces contact but young myopes hate it + RD risk (14% lattice).
Laser PI controversial (maybe early disease).
SLT: low energy, 180° only — big pressure spikes.
Surgery: young myopes prone to hypotony maculopathy.
DDx: PXF (peripupillary TIDs, splotchy pigment), uveitis, iris melanoma, sulcus IOL chafe, BADI.
chunks.hook: Young myopic runner with halos + spoke TIDs = pigment dispersion.

cards.q: Pigment dispersion TIDs vs PXF TIDs?
cards.a: PDS: midperipheral, radial/spoke-like. PXF: peripupillary.

chunks.title: Pseudoexfoliation glaucoma
chunks.tldr: Systemic, age-related; commonest secondary glaucoma in Europeans; 25% risk of glaucoma. Asymmetric/unilateral at presentation. Signs: white flakes on pupil margin, target pattern on anterior capsule (dilate!), peripupillary TIDs, splotchy inferior TM pigment, Sampaolesi line, poor dilation, weak zonules. IOP volatile — can progress in months. SLT works well.
points: Cataract surgery: zonular dialysis, vitreous loss, late IOL dislocation; doesn't cure glaucoma.
Glaucoma: review every 1–3 months; PXF alone: 6–12 months.
DDx: true exfoliation (glassblower, heat), amyloid, UGH.
chunks.hook: Dandruff on the lens = loose zonules + wild pressures.

cards.q: Typical anterior capsule appearance in PXF?
cards.a: Central disc, clear middle zone, peripheral granular zone (target/bull's-eye).

chunks.title: Lens-related glaucomas
chunks.tldr: Phacolytic: hypermature cataract leaks protein through intact capsule → iridescent particles, macrophages, open angle, very high IOP → meds then cataract out within days (24–48 h if uncontrolled). Lens particle: fluffy cortex after trauma/surgery (exclude endophthalmitis). Phacoantigenic: granulomatous uveitis after latent sensitisation. Phacomorphic: big lens closes angle (uniformly shallow AC) → lens extraction. Dislocated lens: pupil block → cycloplegia, lie supine, PI, avoid miotics.
points: B-scan before surgery if no fundus view (tumour/RD).
AC tap shows lens-laden macrophages if doubtful.
Phacolytic with sudden NLP → paracentesis first.
chunks.hook: Old white cataract + sparkling AC + IOP 50 = phacolytic: take the lens out.

cards.q: Key difference between phacolytic and lens particle glaucoma?
cards.a: Phacolytic: intact capsule (hypermature cataract). Lens particle: capsule breached by trauma/surgery.

chunks.title: Plateau iris
chunks.tldr: Anteriorly rotated ciliary body pushes peripheral iris into the angle. Configuration = closes with mild pupil block, PI helps. Syndrome = angle still closes after dilation despite patent PI. Flat central iris, deep central AC, double hump sign on indentation; UBM confirms. Rx: argon iridoplasty, then weak pilocarpine, lens extraction ± ECP.
points: Re-gonio 1 week after PI, then dilate with tropicamide 0.5% and check IOP.
Gonio every 4–6 months; dilate cautiously every ~2 years.
Screen family members.
DDx: pupil block (convex iris bombé), aqueous misdirection (diffusely flat AC).
chunks.hook: Patent PI, still closing = plateau iris → iridoplasty.

cards.q: Gonioscopic sign of plateau iris on indentation?
cards.a: Double hump sign.

chunks.title: Neovascular glaucoma
chunks.tldr: Ischaemia → VEGF → fibrovascular membrane over angle. Stage 1 NVI/NVA, 2 open-angle with high IOP, 3 synechial closure. Causes: PDR, ischaemic CRVO (~90-day glaucoma), CRAO, ocular ischaemic syndrome (carotid Doppler), tumours, chronic RD, uveitis. Rx: steroid + atropine, IOP drops (no pilocarpine, PGA avoided acutely), anti-VEGF now + PRP; tube once quiet; cyclophotocoagulation if poor vision.
points: Treat within 1–2 days — closure progresses over days to weeks.
Anti-VEGF most useful in stages 1–2 while angle still open.
FA guides PRP; B-scan if no view.
Blind painful eye: steroid + atropine may be enough (pain isn't only from IOP).
chunks.hook: Vessels on the iris → anti-VEGF today, PRP this week.

cards.q: No retinal cause for NVI found — next test?
cards.a: Carotid Doppler (ocular ischaemic syndrome).

cards.q: Why is pilocarpine contraindicated in NVG?
cards.a: Breaks down the blood–aqueous barrier, worsening inflammation.

chunks.title: ICE syndrome
chunks.tldr: Unilateral, women 20–50, sporadic. Abnormal endothelium (beaten bronze) migrates over angle → high irregular PAS beyond Schwalbe line, corneal oedema. Three types: essential iris atrophy (holes, corectopia), Chandler (commonest ~50%; oedema even at normal IOP), Cogan–Reese (iris nodules, worst prognosis). Rx: drops, hypertonic saline, tube (long into AC); SLT/PI/MIGS useless; DMEK/PK for oedema.
points: DDx (bilateral, inherited): Axenfeld–Rieger, PPCD, Fuchs, iridoschisis.
Specular microscopy helps.
chunks.hook: One eye, young woman, wandering pupil = ICE.

cards.q: Most common ICE variant?
cards.a: Chandler syndrome.

chunks.title: Postoperative glaucoma & pupil block
chunks.tldr: Early IOP rise after cataract surgery: retained viscoelastic, lens bits, inflammation, hyphaema, pupil block; settles within a week. Treat if >30 (or lower if damaged disc); avoid PGA. Pupil block: iris bombé, no patent PI → YAG PI (often 2); if hazy/inflamed: dilate (cyclopentolate + phenylephrine), aqueous suppressants, steroid. UGH syndrome: IOL chafe → uveitis + glaucoma + hyphaema → atropine, steroid, suppressants, ± reposition/exchange IOL.
points: Other early causes: aqueous misdirection, suprachoroidal haemorrhage, gas/silicone oil, vitreous plug with ACIOL, air behind iris after DMEK.
Late: steroid response, UGH, misdirection when cycloplegia stopped.
UBM shows haptic–ciliary body contact in UGH.
chunks.hook: UGH = Uveitis, Glaucoma, Hyphaema from a rubbing IOL.

cards.q: Most common cause of IOP spike on day 1 after phaco?
cards.a: Retained viscoelastic (also inflammation, debris).

chunks.title: Aqueous misdirection (malignant glaucoma)
chunks.tldr: After surgery in small eyes/angle-closure eyes (or with miotics). Diffusely flat AC (central + peripheral), high IOP, patent PI, no choroidal detachment, no bombé. Aqueous goes backwards into vitreous. Rx: atropine 1% + phenylephrine, CAI, β-blocker, α-agonist, mannitol; miotics contraindicated. If fails: YAG hyaloidotomy/capsulotomy (pseudophakic) or PPV + irido-zonulo-hyaloidectomy (make eye unicameral).
points: B-scan to exclude choroidal effusion/haemorrhage; Seidel for leak.
If broken: atropine daily indefinitely.
Laser PI the fellow eye if occludable.
chunks.hook: Flat everywhere + high IOP + PI open = misdirection → atropine.

cards.q: Drug class contraindicated in aqueous misdirection?
cards.a: Miotics (pilocarpine) — they worsen it; use cycloplegics.

chunks.title: Trabeculectomy complications
chunks.tldr: High IOP + deep AC: blocked internal ostium (iris, blood, fibrin, vitreous) or tight flap → gonio first, Carlo Traverso manoeuvre, laser suture lysis, tPA 10 µg for fibrin. Low IOP (<7; <4 = hypotony risk): overfiltering big bleb (atropine, viscoelastic, autologous blood), flat bleb + flat AC = leak (Seidel), cyclodialysis cleft, serous choroidals. Grade 3 (lens–cornea touch) = emergency → reform AC.
points: AC grading: 1 peripheral iris–cornea, 2 whole iris–cornea, 3 lens–cornea.
Iris in sclerostomy: no massage; pilocarpine/acetylcholine if <2–3 days.
Opening a valveless tube before month 1 → hypotony.
Suprachoroidal haemorrhage: wait ≥10 days before draining if possible.
MMC/5-FU: leaks, thin blebs, scleral melt, blebitis.
Cyclodestruction: hypotony, phthisis, sympathetic ophthalmia.
chunks.hook: Deep chamber + high IOP = blocked. Flat bleb + flat chamber = leaking.

cards.q: Post-trab: flat AC, no bleb, low IOP — first test?
cards.a: Seidel test for wound/bleb leak.

chunks.title: Blebitis
chunks.tldr: Infected bleb, days to years later (MMC, leaks raise risk). Milky bleb, pus in bleb, intense injection. Grade 1 bleb only; 2 + AC cells/hypopyon; 3 + vitritis = bleb-related endophthalmitis. Rx: fortified cefazolin/vancomycin + tobramycin alternating q½h (or FQ q1h) for 1–2; add cycloplegic ± oral moxifloxacin for 2; grade 3 → tap/inject and favour early vitrectomy (fulminant).
points: Early bugs: Staph epidermidis/aureus. Late: Streptococcus, H. influenzae, Moraxella, Pseudomonas.
Re-check at 6–12 h and 12–24 h; daily after; consider admission.
Seidel test the bleb; gonio for microhypopyon.
chunks.hook: Milky bleb = emergency, even years later.

cards.q: Typical organisms in late-onset blebitis?
cards.a: Streptococcus species and Haemophilus influenzae (more virulent).
